references.text: Isaiah's song of the vineyard is the most important Old Testament background for Jesus' parable. The Lord planted a vineyard (Israel) and expected fruit, but found only wild grapes. [ref:Jes 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1-7] uses the vineyard as an image of God's people, just as Jesus here uses the fig tree in the vineyard.

The Lord says through Jeremiah: "I would have gathered them, says the Lord, but there are no grapes on the vine and no figs on the fig tree." [ref:Jer 8:13|Jeremiah 8:13] shows the same motif of a fruitless fig tree as a sign of God's judgment over a people without fruit.

In [ref:Hos 9:10|Hosea 9:10], God compares Israel to the first figs on a fig tree – He found them in the wilderness, but they turned away. The motif of the fig tree as an image of Israel and God's expectation of fruit is central.

The prophet Micah laments: "Woe to me! It is like after the harvest… there is not even one cluster of grapes to eat, no early fig that I long for." [ref:Mi 7:1|Micah 7:1] expresses the same disappointment over lack of fruit, used as an image for the absence of righteous people.

John the Baptist's exhortation in [ref:Luk 3:8-9|Luke 3:8-9] to bear fruit worthy of repentance, and that the axe is already laid at the root of the trees, forms an important background for the parable of the barren fig tree.

The parable of the fig tree follows directly after Jesus' warning in [ref:Luk 13:1-5|Luke 13:1-5] that all must repent or perish. The fruitless fig tree illustrates the consequence of failing to repent.
In [ref:Matt 21:19|Matthew 21:19], Jesus curses a fig tree that bears no fruit, and it withers. This is a symbolic act expressing the same theme as the parable in Luke 13:6 – judgment on barrenness.
Also in [ref:Mark 11:13-14|Mark 11:13-14], Jesus seeks fruit on the fig tree and finds none. The event points to Israel's spiritual barrenness, parallel to the parable in Luke.

In [ref:Joh 15:2-4|John 15:2-4], Jesus speaks of branches that bear no fruit and are cut off. The theme of God's expectation of fruit from His people and the consequence of barrenness connects this to the parable of the fig tree.

In [ref:Rom 11:22|Romans 11:22], Paul speaks of God's kindness and severity – kindness to those who remain in Him, but severity toward those who fall away. This reflects the same dynamic as in the parable, where the owner shows patience but also has a limit.
